title: The Ghetto Sequence Is the Achievement. The Violin Is the Retreat
verdict: Kamiński's handheld camera makes attention a moral act, and then the score and one tinted coat step in to make the decision for the audience it had just trusted.
excerpt: Spielberg gives away his authority over the frame for long stretches of this film, and those stretches are the most formally rigorous work of his career; what surrounds them cannot bear to leave a viewer alone with what has been photographed.
content:
## The camera is a witness, and it is not a steady one

Janusz Kamiński shot this film in black and white, on 35mm, with the camera in someone's hands for much of its length. That decision is the film's argument, and it is made before a word is spoken. A tripod composes. A held camera attends. When the frame shifts slightly because an operator's weight moved, the image admits that a person is present, watching, and could have looked elsewhere.

Spielberg is not usually a director who admits that. His reputation rests on the opposite gift — the ability to place a camera exactly where the emotion is and hold it there until the audience arrives. Here he gives much of that authority away. In the liquidation of the Kraków ghetto, the film stops organising. It follows one figure, loses them, picks up another, hears something off-screen and turns too late. Events happen at the edges. Deep focus keeps the background populated, so a viewer is never permitted the mercy of a shallow plane where only the foreground exists.

This is the most rigorous stretch of filmmaking in Spielberg's work. It respects the ambiguity of a real space by refusing to master it. A sequence that long, that unorganised, that willing to let the viewer's attention fail is a formal achievement, and it is the reason to take the film seriously as cinema rather than as an occasion.

## Deep focus, and a window that will not close

The film is full of frames inside frames — doorways, windows, the slats of a cattle car, the gap between a curtain and a sill. Kamiński repeatedly shoots from inside one room into another, so that an event has a foreground of people who can see it and choose what to do. Oskar Schindler watches through glass a great deal. So does Amon Göth, from a balcony above the camp, and the film gives that balcony the same visual grammar it gives Schindler's window.

That parallel is the film's finest piece of construction and it is achieved by staging rather than by cutting. Two men look down through an opening at people who cannot look back. The composition makes the moral distinction sit inside a physical resemblance, and it does so without a line of dialogue nominating it. Ralph Fiennes plays Göth in full body, in wide shots, doing ordinary things at ordinary speed. Nothing about the framing marks him as an aberration. The film understands that a monster who is photographed like a monster has been let off.

Liam Neeson is used the same way — kept at a distance, in his whole physical bulk, so that the performance is carried by posture and by the way a man occupies a room he has bought his way into. Ben Kingsley works in the opposite register, contained and precise, and the two are frequently in the same frame rather than in alternating close-ups. Coverage would have made their relationship into a series of reactions. Staging makes it a negotiation.

## Where it decides for you

And then the film scores it. John Williams's music, with Itzhak Perlman's violin, arrives to tell a viewer what a scene has already shown them, and the effect is to close a question the images had left open. A held shot in the ghetto sequence asks the audience to do something — to look, to fail to look, to choose. A violin entering under that shot performs the feeling on the audience's behalf, and what was demanded becomes something merely received.

The girl in the red coat is the clearest instance. The film is monochrome; a single figure is tinted, and the eye is instructed. It is an effective device and that is the objection. Until that moment the frame had been crowded with people of equal photographic weight, which is precisely the condition under which a viewer must decide where to look. Colouring one of them removes the decision. The film has been arguing that attention is a moral act, and then it directs the attention itself.

There is a version of this picture that trusts its own camera all the way down. It exists inside this one, in long stretches, and it is remarkable. What surrounds it is a film that cannot finally bear to leave an audience alone with what it has photographed, and so keeps reaching in to guarantee the response.

## Formal seriousness, incompletely kept

The subject does not exempt the method, and it is not disrespect to say so — it is the only form of respect available to criticism. A film about the destruction of people is answerable for how it composes, cuts and scores, more answerable than a film about anything else, because every choice determines what the viewer is permitted to do.

Where the camera attends without organising, this is as serious as narrative cinema has been. Where the music and the tinting step in, it becomes a film that has decided the audience cannot be trusted with its own eyes. Both are present, often within the same reel. Kamiński's ghetto is the achievement, and the score laid over parts of it is the retreat from that achievement.

Half a star lives in that gap.

title: Nobody Warns You That It Is About Your Parents
verdict: The DeLorean gets the poster, but the reason the last act plays like a held breath is that a boy has met his mother and father as teenagers and cannot help liking them.
excerpt: Zemeckis and Gale built a clockwork so smooth that people praise the clock instead of the picture, and the picture is a genuinely moving story about forgiving two people for having once been young and frightened.
content:
## It is a family drama wearing a very good disguise

I have watched this movie more times than is respectable, and every time I am struck by the same thing: nobody warns you that it is about your parents. You come for the car. You stay because a seventeen-year-old boy has to sit in a diner and look at his father as a seventeen-year-old boy, and find out that the man was a coward before he was a disappointment.

That is a real subject. Robert Zemeckis and Bob Gale built a machine around it so smooth that people talk about the machine instead. Fine — the machine is a marvel. But the reason the last act plays like a held breath is not the plutonium. It is that Marty McFly has met his mother and father as kids and he likes them, which is the last thing he expected and the one thing that could hurt him.

## The house tells you everything before anyone speaks

Look at the McFly house in 1985. It is not squalid — it is worse than squalid, it is beaten. The furniture is perfectly adequate. The television is on and nobody is really watching it. Lorraine has a drink and a story she has told before, and Lea Thompson plays her with a kind of glazed sweetness that is the most quietly devastating thing in the movie. Crispin Glover's George laughs at the television at exactly the wrong pitch. In four minutes, without a single line of exposition about the family's history, you know precisely how much life has been surrendered in that room and roughly when.

Then the film takes the same actors, hands them thirty fewer years, and lets you watch them be capable of something. Glover's 1955 George is not a different person; he is the same nervous man before the nervousness set like concrete. Thompson's Lorraine is not a different woman; she is that sweetness with the glaze not yet on. Both performances depend on you having seen the later version first, which is a screenwriting trick of a very high order, and both actors are good enough to make the trick feel like observation.

I keep coming back to Glover's hands. He does something with them — a fold, a retreat — that he does in both time periods, and it is the same gesture at two different pressures. That is an actor thinking.

## Michael J. Fox is doing more work than he gets credit for

Fox has to be the audience's representative and the film's engine at once. He is on screen almost continuously and he is almost always reacting to something absurd, which is the fastest way for a performance to go shrill. He never does. He plays each impossibility as a practical problem: right, that happened, now what. When his eyes change — and they change several times, always a beat before the dialogue admits it — you see a kid recalculating what he thought he knew about the two people who raised him.

Christopher Lloyd is the opposite strategy and it works because Fox is holding the floor. Doc Brown is played at maximum volume with total sincerity, no wink anywhere, and that sincerity is what keeps a cartoon from becoming a smirk. The friendship between them is written thinly and performed thickly. You believe it because both men behave as though they have already had a hundred conversations you were not present for.

Thomas F. Wilson deserves a word too. Biff is a genuinely frightening piece of work in the 1955 scenes — not a comic bully, a real one, with the particular menace of somebody who has never once been told no.

## Every joke pays a debt

The screenplay's reputation as a clockwork is deserved and slightly misdescribed. It is not that everything is a setup for a later payoff, though a great deal is. It is that the setups are all *characterisation* first. A detail that will matter later is introduced as something a person wants, or fears, or cannot stop saying. So the mechanism never feels like a mechanism while it is loading. You are watching people; then later you find out you were also watching a plan.

Alan Silvestri's score gets this. It is enormous — brass piled on brass — and it treats a boy driving a car as an event of historical significance, which from inside the boy's life it is. Zemeckis stages the big sequences with real geography: you always know where the car is, where the clock is, how much road is left. Modern films of this size routinely lose that, and losing it costs them everything Zemeckis banks.

## What it promised, and kept

I grade against the promise a picture makes in its first ten minutes. This one promises a fast, funny, ingeniously constructed entertainment about a kid and a car, and it delivers that completely while smuggling in a story about forgiving your parents for being people. Nothing in it is cruel. Nobody in it is despised, not even Biff, who is simply allowed to be what he is.

There is a scene late on that I will not describe, in which George McFly finally does the thing the whole film has been waiting for him to do, and the audience I saw it with in a full house made a noise I have heard maybe a dozen times in a cinema. Not a laugh. A cheer that starts before the action finishes, because everyone has understood what it will cost him.

Forty-one years on it still gets that noise. That is not nostalgia. That is construction.

title: Watch It for the Dents
verdict: Its power is entirely material — scuffed panels, a scuba regulator's wet rasp, Tunisian glare, an orchestra refusing to apologise — and none of it needs the mythology industry that grew up around it.
excerpt: Everything in this film is dirty, dented and second-hand, and that texture, plus Ben Burtt's junk-built sound and one dry unhurried voice, is where the sensation actually lives.
content:
## Everything in it is dirty

The first fact about this film is not a story. It is a texture.

Surfaces here are scratched, sun-bleached, oil-stained, dented at the corners where something has been knocked against a doorframe too many times. Panels do not fit flush. Paint has come off along the edges that hands touch. The interior of the smuggler's ship is greasy in the way a working kitchen is greasy — not decorated to look used, but built so that use is the only thing you can read off it.

This is the whole achievement, and it is a material one. Science fiction on screen before 1977 was mostly clean: white, seamless, pressurised, hostile to fingerprints. Lucas has his production designers scuff everything. The result is not realism. It is something stranger and more useful — the sensation of having arrived somewhere late, after the interesting events, into a world already worn down by ordinary work. You are not shown a future. You are shown a place with a maintenance history.

Gilbert Taylor lights it flatly and hot in the desert exteriors, shot in Tunisia, where the sand goes almost white and the shadows are short and hard. Then the film descends into interiors lit like submarines. The two palettes never blend. Heat and then metal. Glare and then gloom.

## The sound arrived before the images did

Close your eyes in the first ten minutes and the film still works. That is not a compliment paid to many pictures.

Ben Burtt built these noises out of the physical world rather than an oscillator, and the material origins stay audible. The dark figure's breathing is a scuba regulator, and it retains the wetness of a real apparatus around a real mouth — a rasp with moisture in it, which is why it registers in the body rather than the ear. The energy blades hum with the sound of an idling projector motor crossed with the interference of a television tube. Machines here sound like machines that were once something else. There is grit in the signal.

The small droid does not speak and is the most legible character in the film, because Burtt gave it a vocabulary of pitch and tempo instead of words. Rising and fast is alarm. Descending and slow is refusal. An audience decodes it in under a minute without instruction, which tells you how much of screen character is carried by rhythm alone.

Against all of this: John Williams and the London Symphony Orchestra, playing late-Romantic brass with absolute conviction. The juxtaposition is the film's boldest gesture. Grimy surfaces, junk-built sound effects, and then a full orchestra treating it with the seriousness of Wagner. Nothing about that should hold together. It holds together because neither element apologises.

## Faces, and one voice

Alec Guinness speaks slowly in a film that is otherwise in a hurry, and the tempo change is the most sensuous thing in it. His voice has a dry papery quality — no vibrato, very little volume, consonants placed exactly. He delivers absurd propositions in the register of a man discussing crop rotation. The film's strangeness becomes admissible because one voice in it refuses to be excited.

Carrie Fisher's face is doing something unusual for 1977: she plays irritation as her default state. Not fear, not gratitude. A young woman visibly finding the men around her insufficient. The flatness of her line delivery has been mocked for decades and it is the correct choice — a person under that much pressure who was also emoting would be unbearable.

Harrison Ford's contribution is physical impatience. He is always slightly already leaving. Mark Hamill's is the opposite, an open unguarded face that the camera can point at anything and get a usable reaction from. The film needs one performer with no defences and he supplies it.

## Tempo, and the failure of tempo

The cantina sequence is the picture at its most alive: a fast succession of masks, brief and unexplained, none of them dwelt upon long enough to become an anthropology lesson. The band plays something jaunty and wrong. The camera moves through bodies. Nothing is glossed. It lasts a few minutes and contains more sensation than most films manage in two hours.

The desert middle drags, and it drags in a specific way — the film pauses to arrange its business, and the arranging is visible. There is a stretch on the farm where you can feel information being distributed. Later, in a corridor of grey metal, the movie goes briefly weightless: the surfaces stop being interesting, the tempo becomes uniform, and for a reel the thing is merely competent.

It recovers. The final movement is built almost entirely out of cutting rhythm and sound, and it accelerates without ever losing the physical fact of models photographed against black. I will not describe what happens there. I will say that its intensity comes from editing pattern, not from stakes — the same sequence with the same cuts and no dialogue at all would still raise a pulse.

## Sensation, not meaning

An industry of commentary exists to tell you that this film is really about myth, or about the monomyth, or about the American 1970s. It is not really about anything. It is a surface — sand, grease, brass, breath — assembled at high speed by people who cared enormously how things looked and sounded and not at all how they would be interpreted.

Watch it for the dents. The dents are the argument.
